text: Both equivalents live in the same small ladder: \(V_{Th}\) is the open-circuit voltage across the named pair, and \(R_{Th}\) is the resistance left once the independent sources are dead. Ground the bottom rail, solve the node voltages once, and both parts fall out.

name: Thevenin's theorem
text: A linear two-terminal circuit can be replaced by an equivalent circuit consisting of a voltage source \(V_{Th}\) in series with a resistor \(R_{Th}\), where \(V_{Th}\) is the open-circuit voltage at the terminals and \(R_{Th}\) is the input or equivalent resistance at the terminals when the independent sources are turned off.

title: Ground c and name the node voltages

text: Take the bottom rail, terminal c, as the reference node \(V_c = 0\). Name the junction above the 24 V source \(V_1\), the junction where the 3 Ω, 1 Ω and 4 Ω meet \(V_2\), and the junction of the 4 Ω, 5 Ω and 2 A source \(V_b\) (Fig. 4.111, p. 165). For the open-circuit voltage nothing external is attached to a or b, so the 1 Ω running out to terminal a carries no current: **terminal a sits at node 2's potential**, \(V_a = V_2\).

title: Write KCL at the three live nodes

text: The 24 V source and the 2 Ω form one series branch with nothing tapping their joint, so the current down that branch is \((V_1 - 24)/2\): leaving node 1 you first drop 24 V through the source, then cross the 2 Ω. Summing currents out of each node to zero gives:

steps.why: KCL at node 1: the current down the source-plus-2 Ω branch plus the current right through the 3 Ω.
KCL at node 2, with the 1 Ω out to the open terminal a dropped since it carries no current.
KCL at node b: the 2 A source pushes current up into b, and the 4 Ω and 5 Ω carry it away.
No current through the 1 Ω means no voltage drop across it.
Equation (4.6) defines the Thevenin voltage as the open-circuit voltage, positive at a [p. 137].

text: It makes sense that a ends up above b: the network between the terminals is active, and it would push current out of a if a load were hung there.

The solution also reads as a tidy current story. The source branch carries \((22 - 24)/2 = -1\) A; the minus sign means 1 A actually flows up into node 1. That 1 A crosses the 3 Ω, \((22 - 19)/3 = 1\) A, then the 4 Ω, \((19 - 15)/4 = 1\) A, while the 1 Ω to a idles. At node b the 2 A source joins it, \(1 + 2 = 3\) A, and the 5 Ω takes it all down to c, \(15/5 = 3\) A. Every node balances.

title: Turn off the sources and combine resistors

text: This circuit has no dependent sources, so CASE 1 applies [p. 138]: turn off the independent sources, the 24 V source becoming a short circuit and the 2 A source an open circuit. What is left between a and b is a dead resistor ladder. Looking in from a, the 1 Ω is in series with node 2's view of b, and node 2 reaches b two ways: straight down the 4 Ω, or across the 3 Ω, through the shorted source's 2 Ω to ground, and back up the 5 Ω.

steps.why: Equation (4.7): the input resistance of the dead network, the 1 Ω in series with the two parallel node-2-to-b paths.
Parallel elements combine by reciprocal addition.

title: Cross-check with \(R_{Th} = v_{oc}/i_{sc}\)
text: The book offers exactly this check [p. 138]. Short a to b and re-solve the same three nodes, the 1 Ω now feeding the short: the short-circuit current comes out \(i_{sc} = 28/27 \approx 1.037\) A from a to b. Then \(v_{oc}/i_{sc} = 4/(28/27) = 27/7\ \Omega\), the same resistance found two ways.

title: Read the open-circuit voltage at b-c

text: Nothing external is attached in either part, so the open-circuit circuit for b-c is exactly the one already solved in part (a): terminal a still dangles and all node voltages stand. The open-circuit voltage across b-c is just node b measured above the reference rail c:

steps.why: Same circuit, new terminals: c is the reference node, so \(V_c = 0\), and the + of the equivalent source is at b [p. 137].

title: Combine the dead resistors from b to c

text: Kill the sources again, shorting the 24 V and opening the 2 A [p. 138]. The change from part (a) is the role of the 1 Ω: it now runs from node 2 out to terminal a, a dead end with nothing attached. A resistor with one end open carries no current, so **it drops out of the reduction entirely**. From b to ground two paths remain: the 5 Ω straight down, or up the 4 Ω, across the 3 Ω, and down the 2 Ω to ground.

steps.why: The two b-to-ground paths sit in parallel between the terminals.

title: Why the two equivalents differ
text: The circuit never changed; only the viewing window did. Across b-c you read node b's full 15 V, while across a-b you catch only the 4 V step from a down to b. The resistance reshuffles too: at a-b the 1 Ω sat in series with the input while the 4 Ω was one of two parallel paths; at b-c the 1 Ω dangles off node 2 and vanishes, while the 4 Ω joins the 3 Ω and 2 Ω in series against the 5 Ω.

A final cross-check for b-c: short b to c and re-solve the two remaining nodes. Node 2 lands at \(V_2 = \frac{32}{3}\ \text{V}\), and the short carries \(i_{sc} = 2 + \frac{32/3}{4} = \frac{14}{3}\) A down from b to c, the 2 A source plus \(V_2/4\) arriving through the 4 Ω. Then \(v_{oc}/i_{sc} = 15/(14/3) = \frac{45}{14}\ \Omega\), matching the ladder [p. 138].
